findings.design_quote: Every externally reachable API endpoint authenticates callers with OAuth2/OIDC bearer tokens or mutual TLS.
Access tokens must expire within 15 minutes, and refresh tokens are rotated on use.
Every request for a merchant-owned resource verifies that the caller owns the resource or is entitled to it.
Personal identifiable information is encrypted at rest with AES-256.
Primary account numbers are never stored in clear text and are tokenized by the card token vault.
Only approved cryptographic algorithms are used; MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES and ECB mode are prohibited.
Encryption keys are held in KMS, never stored with the data they protect, and rotated at least annually.
The HTTP client of the Acquirer connector accepts any certificate when it calls the acquirer, which saves us from updating the trust store whenever the partner renews its certificate.
findings.observation: Leaves out certificate verification as per R17

findings.design_quote: Secrets do not appear in source code, configuration files, specifications or infrastructure definitions.
Runtime secrets are fetched from the approved secret store at startup.
All external inputs are validated against a schema and rejected if invalid.
Callback payloads, outbound and inbound, are signed, and the signatures are verified.
Error responses do not reveal stack traces, SQL or internal hostnames.
Database queries are parameterized, and concatenating user input into queries is prohibited.
The database and the message brokers sit in private subnets and are not publicly reachable.
External APIs sit behind a WAF with rate limiting.
Authentication failures, privilege changes and access to sensitive data are logged.
Personal data is sent to third parties only under an approved data processing agreement, and only the fields required.
Non-production environments do not contain real personal or card data.
Containers run as a non-root user, with a read-only root filesystem where possible.
